10709-prince-zaleski:
Matthew Phipps Shiel published Prince Zaleski in 1895, three tales of detection centered on an exiled prince. Zaleski, victim of an unfortunate love and exile from his native land, has renounced the world, yet his just and passionate mind still solves mysteries others cannot. The cases are "The Race of Orven," "The Stone of the Edmundsbury Monks," and "The S.S."

Shiel writes in rich, ornate prose, with a hero who reasons from his solitude like a philosopher-detective. The stories predate much of the detective fashion and carry a decadent flavor. Readers who like Poe and early crime fiction will find here a strange, brilliant forerunner.
22046-maxim-gorki:
Hans Ostwald's study of Maxim Gorki introduced German readers to the new voice in Russian letters. Gorki, whose name means "the bitter one," had risen from tramp and baker to famous writer. Ostwald says a memorable note had sounded through Russian literature, quickening the whole. Russian readers welcomed Gorki first, and foreign readers soon followed.

The book sketches Gorki's hard early life and the tramps, workers, and outcasts who fill his tales. Ostwald treats him as the spokesman of Russia's lowest depths. At the time, Gorki's plays and stories were a European sensation. This early study shows how his fame looked to a foreign critic before the Russian Revolution.
23362-mademoiselle-olympe-zabriski:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich opens this tale with a defence of male gossip, praising Samuel Pepys as king of tattlers and backing his own club against any women's club for chat. From that droll start, the story turns to Mademoiselle Olympe Zabriski, a young woman whose name and looks set tongues wagging.

Club men trade tales, hints, and guesses about her, and Aldrich lets their talk build a portrait that may owe more to fancy than to fact. The tale is a comedy of report: how a reputation grows in drawing rooms, how wit sharpens it, and how little truth a good story needs. Its fun lies in watching smart men prove, at length, that they gossip just as well as anyone.
24637-bromide-printing-and-enlarging-a-p:
Published by Tennant and Ward at New York in 1912, this practical guide covers bromide printing and enlarging. Its chapters take up varieties of bromide paper and how to choose among them, the question of light, contact prints, and enlarging by daylight and by artificial light.

Later chapters treat dodging, vignetting, composite printing, the use of bolting silk, and the reduction and toning of prints and enlargements. The guide is written for photographers working in the darkroom. Readers interested in old photographic craft will find it a clear, detailed handbook of a vanished art.
685-the-atomic-bombings-of-hiroshima-and:
The Manhattan Engineer District issued this official report on 29 June 1946, less than a year after the atomic attacks on Japan. It sums up what survey teams found in the two ruined cities, from the choice of targets to the scale of damage and injury. A foreword, a survey of the project, and a set of main findings frame the account.

The report describes each city before the attack, then each blast, then the wreck of buildings, the fires, and the harm to people, with a direct comparison of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Its sober, factual tone makes it a key first-hand source. It lets readers judge the human and physical cost of the new weapon from the record made by those sent to measure it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-krzyck:
Andrew Krzycki, Polish-Latin poet, died in 1535; his birth date is uncertain. A supple courtier, he treated poetry as a source of renown and profit. Well-read in Latin poetry, he knew the language to perfection and wrote epigrams. His talent, confined to imitations of the ancients, was significant, and his wit was mordant and at times coarse.

His verses mostly commemorated notable occasions. In 1512 he celebrated Sigismund I's marriage to Barbara Zapolya, then became chancellor to the queen. After Orsza he sent verses, purporting to be from the queen to her absent husband after Ovid's Epistolae Heroidum, which Erasmus praised enthusiastically. After Barbara's death he served Bona Sforza, took orders, and obtained benefices and a bishopric. The spreading Reformation dismayed him and occasioned his serious work, Religions et Reipublicae quaerimonia (1522). He rose to Primate Archbishop of Gnesen, and his last work, De Asiana Dieta, criticized the turbulent diet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-casimir-pulas:
Casimir Pulaski was a Polish patriot and soldier born at Winiary in March 1748 who died aboard the Wasp in Savannah harbor in October 1779. His father, a jurist, raised him for the bar, but he trained with the guard of Charles, Duke of Courland. With his father he helped form the Confederation of Bar in February 1768 to free Poland from Russia. He seized Berdichev monastery and held it for weeks against a Russian siege.

After his father's arrest and death in 1769, Pulaski's marches raised much of Poland and Lithuania. Suvaroff beat him at Lomazy, and he fled with ten men to the Carpathians. He seized Czenstochowa in August 1770 and held it against a Russian siege in January 1771. In America he offered his services to Franklin in October 1776 and joined Washington. He won brigadier rank for horse in September 1777. He fell wounded leading American and French cavalry at Savannah in October 1779.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-uje:
Stanislaus Tarnowski's entry treats Cornelius Ujejski, Polish poet. Born at Beremiany, Galicia, in 1823, he died at Cholojewie in 1897. While still a student there, Ujejski wrote Maraton in 1843, a patriotic lyric of excellent form. In 1846, at the Austrian Government's instigation, Galician peasants massacred several thousand nobles.

Ujejski voiced universal indignation in his powerful poem Choral, which became Poland's national hymn. At Paris in 1847 he published Skargi Jeremiego, Lamentations of Jeremias. He met the Polish colony's leading men at Paris, among them Mickiewicz, devoting himself to the poet Julius Slowacki. Returning home in 1848, he won great popularity as the people's national poet. Other fine poems followed, including Kwiaty bez woni, Flowers without perfume, 1848, and Zwiedle liscie, Faded leaves, 1849. In 1852 he published Melodye Biblijne, Biblical Melodies. He never surpassed his youthful works, though later poems show patriotic feeling and fine taste.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fabian-birkow:
Fabian Birkowski was a Polish preacher, born at Lemberg in 1566 and dead at Cracow in 1636. He studied at the University of Cracow, where he began teaching philosophy in 1587. After five years there he entered the Dominican Order in 1592 and dug deeper into theology. He then preached at Holy Trinity church in Cracow, where the king worshipped.

For fourteen years his fame drew immense crowds. Sigismund III prized him, consulted him on temporal and spiritual matters, and took him to Warsaw when the court moved. The king also made him his son Wladislaw's court preacher. In the 1617 and 1618 campaigns against Turks, Russians, and Walachians, the friar played no small part, preaching to soldiers in camp. He ranks among Poland's greatest orators, called the Sarmatian Chrysologus, unmatched in purity of diction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaspar-druzbi:
Gaspar Druzbicki, a Polish Jesuit ascetic writer born at Sieradz in 1589, spent his life forming novices and ruling colleges. He entered the Society in 1609, taught for some years, then served as master of novices and rector at Kalisz, Ostrog, and Posen. Twice provincial, he sat in the order's seventh and tenth general congregations before his death at Posen in 1662.

Nearly all his books appeared after his death, drawn from his Ascetic Works, too tangled to order by date. They include meditations on Christ's life and Passion, a Tribunal of Conscience, Considerations for Sundays and feasts, and The Sacred Heart, the Goal of Hearts. A full list of his writings fills twelve columns in Sommervogel's bibliography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignatius-kras:
Ignatius Krasicki was a Polish bishop and writer, born in 1735 and dead at Berlin in 1801. He took orders in youth and soon became a canon. He travelled abroad and gave the coronation sermon for King Stanislaus Poniatowski, whose favour soon won him a bishopric in what soon became Prussian Poland. Frederick II then befriended him, and to amuse that king, it is said, Krasicki wrote his Monachomachia.

In 1775 appeared his heroicomic poem Myszeis, the Mousiad, a purposely tangled allegory on Poland's state. A bishop, the entry argues, ought rather to have reformed monks than laughed at them, and writing for a Protestant king's amusement was a graver blunder if the charges were true. Krasicki felt the sting and wrote his Anti-Monachomachia to undo the bad impression, besides a novel, Doswiadczynski, under English fiction's influence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jan-kochanows:
Polish poet Jan Kochanowski was born at Sycyna in 1530 and died at Lublin on 22 August 1584. He enrolled at Cracow university in 1544 but left on account of plague. He studied at Padua in 1552 under the best teachers. There he wrote many Latin elegies imitating Tibullus and Propertius. Thence he traveled to France, where he lived until his mother's death in 1557, writing more and better Latin poetry.

On returning to Poland he received his Czarnolas inheritance and served for a time as courtier, first of great lords, then at the royal court. During that period he produced, with his best Latin elegies, his Polish songs and Fraszki, or trifles. The songs are the first really inspired poetry to appear in Poland. The Fraszki, comical and witty but sometimes coarse, instructively show social life of the time. His Zgoda and Satyr followed. The entry presents Poland's first great vernacular poet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-laski:
John Laski, or Alasco, was Archbishop of Gnesen and Primate of Poland at the dawn of the Reformation. Born at Lask in 1456, he served the royal chancellor and became provost and canon. He was then royal secretary in 1502, arch-chancellor in 1505, coadjutor of Gnesen in 1509, and archbishop and primate on his predecessor's death in 1510.

At the Fifth Lateran Council in 1513 he urged the pope to act against the Teutonic Knights, who had intrigued against Poland since 1466. Leo X made him and his successors legates born in 1515. His elevation to the cardinalate was said to have been blocked by King Sigismund. A zealous upholder of discipline and a strenuous foe of Protestantism, he held provincial synods at Piotrkow and Lencicz through the 1520s. He edited their canons and his own statutes for the Polish Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-sobieski:
John Sobieski was the Polish king whose relief of Vienna in 1683 made him a hero of Christendom. Born at Olesko in 1629, son of the Castellan of Cracow, descendant of Zolkiewski, he fought beside his brother Mark. He fought from the Cossack rebellion of 1648 until Mark's murder by Tatars at Batoh. Faithful to King John Casimir against Lubomirski's revolt, he rose to field hetman, grand marshal, and grand hetman.

At Podhajce he raised eight thousand men at his own expense and baffled Cossacks and Tatars. At Chocim his victory cost the Turks twenty thousand men and many guns. On Michael's death he was unanimously elected king in 1674. At Zurawno he wore out a Turkish army ten times his own and regained much of Ukraine by treaty. When a Turkish host marched on Vienna in 1683 and Leopold fled, Sobieski's relief of the city crowned his career as the Unvanquished Northern Lion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-dabrow:
Joseph Dabrowski was a Polish priest who founded the Detroit seminary for Polish Americans. Born in Russian Poland, he fought in the Polish rising of 1863, fled to Dresden and Switzerland, and was ordained in Rome in 1869 under the Resurrectionist Father Semenenko. He reached America in 1870 and saw at once the disordered state of Polish immigrant life.

As pastor at Polonia, Wisconsin, he rebuilt church buildings twice after fire and brought the Felician Sisters from Cracow to teach Polish children. Entrusted with a Polish seminary plan, he began building at Detroit in 1884, opened the school in 1887, and led it as rector for nineteen years until his death in 1903.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-szujsk:
Joseph Szujski was a Polish historian and poet who taught his nation to face its own faults. Born at Tarnow in 1835, he studied at Cracow and Vienna, began as a poet and dramatist, and turned to history with a manual whose later volumes show true research. The failed rising of 1863 drove him to seek the causes of Poland's misfortunes.

His 1865 work Some Truths of Our History declared that no nation falls except through its own fault, and none rises except by its own intelligent labor. Named professor of Polish history at Cracow in 1869 and later rector, he led the Academy of Sciences as secretary from 1872. He died of consumption at Cracow in 1883.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcin-bielsk:
Marcin Bielski, also called Wolski, was a Polish chronicler born at Biala in 1495 and dead there in 1575. His family name came from Biala, and Wolski from his estate at Wola. He was the first of two Polish writers of the name to write in Polish, and so counts as father of Polish prose.

He studied at Cracow University, served with the city's military governor, and fought Wallachians and Tatars, including at Obertyn in 1531. His works include Lives of the Philosophers of 1535 and a Universal Chronicle of 1550 to 1564. It was the first major universal history in Polish, with a first attempt at a full history of Poland from 550 to 1580. A second edition of 1554 mentions America. His son Joachim later carried the chronicle to 1597 as the Chronicle of Poland. A treatise on warfare of 1569 and satirical poems after his death complete a remarkably fruitful output.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mathias-casim:
Mathias Casimir Sarbiewski, the Horace of Poland, was born near Plonsk in Masovia in 1595 and died in 1649. He entered the Vilna Jesuit novitiate in 1612, studied rhetoric and philosophy in 1614 to 1617, and taught grammar, humanities, and rhetoric. He studied theology at Vilna and Rome, and was ordained at Rome in 1623.

Back in Poland he taught rhetoric, philosophy, and theology at Vilna from 1626 to 1635, then became preacher to King Wladislaw and travelled with him four years. His fame spans the world of letters. Gifted broadly, above all in music and fine arts, his chief excellence lay as a poet versed in every ancient metre. He loved Horace, memorising his odes, and wrote Latin verse that earned him the Polish Horace title. Select poems have been translated from Latin into many tongues, and his Poemata Omnia appeared at Starawies in 1812. He remains Poland's classic lyric voice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miecislas-hal:
Miecislas Halka Ledochowski, count, cardinal, and Archbishop of Gnesen-Posen, was born at Gorki near Sandomir in Russian Poland on 29 October 1822 and died at Rome on 22 July 1902. After studying at Radom and Warsaw, he entered Rome's Accademia dei Nobili Ecclesiastici in 1842 and was ordained priest on 13 July 1845. He became domestic prelate of Pius IX in 1846 and auditor of the Lisbon nunciature in 1847.

He served as apostolic delegate to Colombia and Chile in 1856, and nuncio at Brussels and titular Archbishop of Thebes in 1861. He became Archbishop of Gnesen-Posen in December 1865, enthroned on 22 April 1866. On friendly terms with the King of Prussia, he was sent to Versailles during the Franco-Prussian War. His later clash with Bismarck's Kulturkampf, imprisonment, and elevation to the cardinalate made him a symbol of Polish Catholic resistance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nagasaki:
Nagasaki, capital of the prefecture of the same name, stands on a small peninsula on the southeastern coast of Kiushiu, Japan. Its harbour, ringed on three sides by mountains and sheltered at its mouth by islands, ranks among the safest and most important in Japan. It is a leading coaling station of the Far East, first port of entry from south and west, with engine works and shipbuilding as chief industries.

In the first ten centuries it bore at least seven names, best known Fukaye no Ura. Its present name likely comes from Nagasaki Kotaro, who held it as fief about 1185 to 1190. Before the missionaries it was an insignificant village. Saint Francis Xavier laboured in the territory now forming the diocese. The entry follows Nagasaki through the early Japanese church, persecution, the hidden Christians, and the modern diocese's parishes and missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rimouski:
Rimouski is a diocese at the eastern tip of Quebec, suffragan to the archdiocese of Quebec. It takes in the counties of Bonaventure, Gaspe, Rimouski, and most of Temiscouata. Jacques Cartier landed at the Gaspe point on his first voyage in 1534 and planted a cross bearing the arms of France. Micmac people along the Baie des Chaleurs were served in turn by Recollets, Capuchins, Jesuits, and Spiritans, including Pierre Maillard.

The first Mass near Rimouski was said by the Jesuit Henri Nouvel in 1663 at a place later called Pointe-au-Pere. Germain Lepage settled Rimouski in 1696, and his family name became the diocese's titular. The see was created on 15 January 1867, with Jean-Pierre-Francois Laforce-Langevin as first bishop. He organized a classical college as the diocesan seminary, brought in teaching sisters, and approved the Sisters of the Most Holy Rosary in 1879. Recent figures count 120 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sigismund-kra:
Sigismund Krasinski, Count and son of a Polish general, was born at Paris on 19 February 1812 and died there on 23 February 1859. He lost his mother, Princess Radziwill, in childhood. At school in Warsaw he shone as a sympathizer with the Romantic movement. When he held back from political demonstrations in 1829 to obey his father, fellow students turned so hostile that his father sent him to Geneva.

Intensely patriotic, he suffered during the insurrection of 1831, and his health broke when he was forced to present himself at Tsar Nicholas's court. Allowed to withdraw to Vienna, he published his first great work. The Undivine Comedy of 1833 stages the struggle of old order and new, each with a faithless champion, both ending in despair. Irydion of 1836 follows a young Greek who dreams of freeing his country from Rome, fails in vengeance, and is judged by Christ for evil deeds and want of trust.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-starowo:
Simon Starowolski, born at Stara Wola near Cracow in 1585, died at Cracow in 1656. He studied at Louvain but took his degrees at Cracow University, then traveled across western Europe. Returning, he taught philosophy at Cracow and became secretary to Chodkiewicz, whom he followed on the Chocim expedition. For years he tutored young noblemen, traveling Europe again with the son of Hetman Koniecpolski. Ordained priest in 1639, he later became a canon of Cracow.

During the Swedish siege of 1655 he ran the diocese for Bishop Gebicki, and it fell to him to show the cathedral to the Swedish king. Pointing to the tomb of Lokietek, thrice an exile and thrice returned, he drew Charles Gustavus's remark that John Casimir would never return. Fortuna variabilis, Deus immutabilis, he answered: fortune changes, God does not. He died months later, before John Casimir's triumphant return. His writings ranged across history, law, theology, politics, and literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanislaus-ko:
Stanislaus Konarski, a Piarist reformer of Polish schools, believed political reform must follow reform of education. Born in 1700 and dead in 1773, he visited Rome after ordination and there first grasped his life's mission. Returning through France and Germany, studying their school systems on the way, he at first failed in his plans and compiled the Volumina Legum, its first volume appearing in 1732.

During the interregnum after Augustus II he wrote for Stanislaus Leszczynski, then travelled in the Netherlands and France, staying at the exiled king's court. Convinced that politics must wait on schooling, he returned home in 1738, trained teachers as master of novices at Rzeszów, and sent them as tutors or abroad at his own cost. In 1740 he opened Warsaw's Collegium Nobilium, an experiment that reshaped Polish education. Its first year held one pupil, its second many more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanislaus-zo:
Stanislaus Zolkiewski, chancellor of Poland, served three kings as soldier and statesman and died on campaign. Born at Turynka in Red Russia in 1547, he studied at Lwów with distinction and reportedly knew all of Horace by heart. With his friend Zamoyski he fought under Stephen Báthory against Ivan the Terrible, winning high favour and becoming castellan of Lwów in 1593.

Sigismund III mistrusted him from the outset and rejected his advice. When Cossacks revolted, Zolkiewski urged gentle treatment but obeyed orders against Nalewajko and Toba. During Zebrzydowski's rising he backed the king despite just noble grievances and beat the rebels at Guzów. Against war with Muscovy over the False Demetrius he warned in vain, yet led the army when ordered. He died at Cecora on 6 October 1620.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanislaw-kar:
Stanislaw Karnkowski, archbishop of Gniezno and primate of Poland, guided church and state through the Reformation's advance. Born about 1526, he was named bishop of Włocławek in 1563, or 1568 by Gams's reckoning, and served religion and education by founding schools and a priests' seminary at his residence. By order of Piotrków's synod in 1577 he compiled synodal laws as Constitutiones synodorum, published at Cracow in 1579.

Under Sigismund II Augustus, Calvinism spread while Lutherans and Socinians fought each other. When Sigismund died, Henry of Valois was elected king, and Karnkowski welcomed him at Międzyrzecz in the estates' name. He attended the coronation in 1574 and tried to keep the new king in Poland, but that year France's throne fell vacant and Henry fled. Karnkowski died at Łowicz on 25 May, or 8 June by another account, 1603.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vespasian-koc:
Wespazjan Kochowski was a Polish historian and poet who lived from 1633 to 1699. Educated at the Jesuit college in Sandomir, he served in the army and then retired to his estate. King Sobieski valued him so highly as a historian that he took him on the famous expedition to Vienna. His literary fruit was a Latin commentary on the war against the Turks, judged among the best chronicles of his time and country.

His short poems, collected as Busy Idleness, range from religion to coarse fun, with simple, noble love poems, laments for his brother, and witty satires. A religiously patriotic tone runs through all, crowned by his original Psalmody, where prayer slides into accounts of the Turkish wars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincent-barzy:
Vincent Barzynski was a Polish Resurrectionist priest who died at Chicago in 1899. Born at Sulislawice in Russian Poland in 1838, baptized Michael, he took the name Vincent after being placed under St Vincent Ferrer's protection during a grave illness. Educated privately for frail health, he entered Lublin seminary in 1856 and was ordained in 1861.

As organizer for the secret Polish national government he supplied insurgents during the 1863 uprising, then fled to Cracow's Franciscans, wandered fifteen months, and left for Paris in 1865. There mystics Semenenko, Kajsiewicz, Jelowicki, and the poet Mickiewicz, dreaming of Poland's rebirth through spiritual regeneration, influenced him. Joining the Resurrectionists at Rome with Pius IX's blessing, he sailed for America in 1866, labouring in Texas before his Chicago pastorate, whose story the entry continues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zbigniew-oles:
Zbigniew Olesnicki was a Polish cardinal and statesman, born in Poland in 1389 and dead at Sandomir on 1 April 1455. At twenty he served as secretary to King Jagello and fought beside him at Grünwald on 14 July 1410. On 9 July 1423 he took the see of Cracow, and in 1433 the king sent him as legate to the Council of Basle, where he sought friendly terms with both parties.

On 18 December 1439 Eugene IV made him cardinal priest of Saint Prisca; the claim that he also accepted the dignity from antipope Felix V has lately been attacked. As cardinal his influence in Poland ranked second only to the king's, and during Casimir IV's frequent absences in Lithuania he ran the state. A man of great learning, he advanced arts and letters in every way, and Cracow University's flourishing state under him is chiefly his work.
doe-osti-2997408-summer-internship-repor: ARA2 benchmarking got its intern report, and this DOE summer text covers the benchmarking work. The pages detail the findings. The program gets its highlight. The report was summer internship. The work was benchmarking. The program got highlights. The highlight was program.
doe-osti-3011874-bypassing-fast-time-sca: Hodgkin-Huxley got fast-bypassed, and this DOE text resets neurons with thresholds. The pages detail the model findings. The neuro folks get their method. The reset was hard. The method was neuro. The model was neuron. The scales were fast.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KingAG-DAGRecor:
A summons issued in Civil Action 76-1185 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia opens a lawsuit by the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. The defendants are FBI officials: Clarence Kelley, the Bureau's director, Cartha DeLoach, William Sullivan, and others. A summons is the paper that drags a defendant into court.

Martin Luther King's own organization suing the FBI's leadership was a landmark confrontation. The Bureau had surveilled King for years, and his movement answered in federal court. The summons preserves the suit's formal start, the civil rights movement taking the Bureau by name.
nasa-tm-19700005657-two-step-mechanism-f:
Robert F. Mueller of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this paper in November 1969. It deals with silicates, the minerals that make up much of Earth's rock. Mueller asks why atoms in these minerals settle into ordered patterns at some temperatures and stay disordered at others.

He proposes that ordering happens in two steps, one after the other. That two-step path, he argues, explains the high energy barrier seen at the lower temperature limit for ordering. It also explains traits that set three kinds of pyroxene rock apart. Below that limit, he says, order can form only when the rock recrystallizes, not by heating alone.
podcast-joerogan-yVHcBcSicKI:
Fresh UFO headlines get a careful review in this Joe Rogan Experience segment with Jacques Vallee. Vallee, the veteran French researcher, weighs new footage and claims as they break. Rogan brings the stories, and Vallee brings a sober, trained eye to each one.

The two sort recent cases into the credible, the doubtful, and the plainly fake. Vallee explains what details he looks for before trusting any report. He also notes how media hype now distorts the field he helped build. Watchers of the strange get a calm check on the noise, from a man who has seen cycles of it before.
prince-zaleski:
M. P. Shiel published Prince Zaleski in 1895 and dedicated it to his dear mother. The contents list three cases only: the Race of Orven, the Stone of the Edmundsbury Monks, and the S.S. The narrator opens by remembering his friend with grief: Zaleski was undone by a love too insistent and too unlucky for even a throne to shame. He renounced the world in exile and was quickly forgotten by it, until the Pharanx labyrinth puzzle drew the narrator back to his hermitage.

What he finds is detective fiction's strangest address: a ruined palace, an organ, a mummy in an open sarcophagus, cannabis fumes. Curios from every age crammed around a couch of cloth of silver, where the prince solves crimes he never visits by pure, passionate reasoning. Shiel invented the decadent detective in three stories; Zaleski has been a cult ever since.
the-atomic-bombings-of-hiroshima-and-nag:
The Manhattan Engineer District issued this report on June 29, 1946, less than a year after the attacks it studies. Its index lays out the plan: a foreword, an introduction, the Manhattan Project investigating group, a propaganda section, a summary of damages and injuries, and the main conclusions. Then come the choosing of the target and pictures of the two cities before the bombings.

Separate accounts treat the attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, followed by a general comparison of the two. Long sections study the nature of an atomic explosion. They treat blast pressure and ground shock. They also treat shielding from blast and flash. A further set studies injuries done to persons: burns, wounds from force, and radiation harm. An appendix adds Father Siemes's eyewitness account.
